Before you start

A book about hands does not need a face. It needs someone who decides to begin.

Hi, I'm Maria Costa, and I'll be your companion over the next few pages. I've been working in marketing since 2013 and, over the last few years, I've focused mostly on info products: guides, templates, planners and small courses that people buy to solve a specific problem. This book comes from a question people ask me all the time: "Maria, can you sell on social media without showing yourself?" You can. But the short answer hides a lot of work, and that's what you're about to read.

What this book is

This is a practical book. It isn't loose theory or a manifesto about freedom. Each chapter has one central idea, an image that helps you remember it, and at least one exercise you have to do with your hands, with a pen or on your phone. Reading alone isn't enough.

By the end, I want you to have three things: a faceless brand that makes sense for you, a first product designed around the person who is going to buy it, and a routine of content and conversations you can keep up without burning out. Nobody can keep posting every day for months while pretending to enjoy it. We're going to do something smaller and more sustainable.

I call it Just the Hands because that's what you'll see in your posts: hands writing, packing, moving across a screen, holding a cup of coffee at seven in the morning. A face isn't compulsory. What sells is what those hands build and show.

What this book is not

I want to be clear from the start:

  • It is not a promise of income. I won't tell you how much you'll earn each month or how long it will take. That depends on your time, your product, your audience and work that only you can do. Results depend on each person's effort.
  • It is not financial, tax or legal advice. When I talk about IRS, invoicing or contracts, I'm giving you general guidance. For specific decisions, speak to a certified accountant or a lawyer.
  • It is not a magic formula. There's no trick that replaces consistency.

I use examples with numbers so we can do the maths, but I always label them "illustrative example". They are not anyone's results. The people in the stories are also fictional, inspired by situations you see every day, not real biographies.

How to use each chapter

The chapters are numbered from 00 to 11, and the order matters, because each one builds on the one before. I suggest one chapter a week, but go at your own pace. Some people take a month and some take three. Both are fine.

You'll find some special blocks. The highlight holds the key idea of the chapter:

Key idea

A key idea, in two or three sentences. If you only keep one thing from a chapter, keep this one.

The exercises have numbered steps and space to write. The alerts warn you about common mistakes. There are also posts, phone screens and conversations, designed to read as if they came from your own phone. When one of these appears, read it slowly, as if it were meant for you.

There's no right answer. The question is there so you can look at the time you have before deciding how much you can give to this.

Before you move on: the notebook

Choose a notebook (or a document on your computer, if you prefer) and call it "Hands Diary". This is where you'll write your answers to the exercises. In four weeks you'll want to read what you wrote today, and you'll see the path you've taken.

Exercise · Your starting point
  1. Write, in one sentence, why you want to sell without showing yourself.
  2. Write, in one sentence, what you already do well and that someone might want to learn or receive from you.
  3. Write how many hours a week you can realistically give to this, without counting the weeks when you're full of energy.
  4. Write what frightens you most about this path. Not so you can judge the fear. So you can get to know it.

Write here:

A note on the word "faceless"

Faceless means, literally, "without a face". In the way I use it, it's a brand where the person behind it exists, works and can be seen, but where the focus is on the process, the product, the hands and the value being delivered. It isn't about hiding yourself. It's about choosing where to shine the light.

Some people say faceless is a trick to avoid exposure. I think it's an honest way of deciding what you share. You decide how much of your personal life goes on the screen, and that is your right, not a flaw.

There are weeks when you miss showing your face and others when you're glad you don't have to. Both feelings are normal.

Rita, 38, a hairdresser in Leiria, is a fictional character. This is the conversation you might have with someone like her at the start:

In summary

  • This book is practical: each chapter has an idea, an image and an exercise.
  • There are no income promises. The examples with numbers are illustrative.
  • The cases are fictional, and results always depend on each person's effort.
  • Use a notebook to keep your answers. You'll need them.

To do today

  1. Open your notebook or the notes app on your phone and write "Hands Diary" at the top, with today's date.
  2. Do the exercise "Your starting point". You don't need to be perfect. Write the four answers in twenty minutes, even if they're short.
  3. Read the answer to the last question out loud. If it feels uncomfortable, note beside it why.
  4. Leave the notebook somewhere you'll see it tomorrow morning.
1

Why the face isn't the product

A face catches the eye. Hands show that there's work behind it.

Anyone who has worked in marketing for a while notices something odd. The people who buy the most rarely buy the face of the person selling. They buy the solution to a problem they have that week: the spreadsheet that won't add up, the training plan they never manage to stick to, the list of content ideas stuck in their head. The face was, almost always, a detail.

This chapter takes apart the idea that, to sell online, you have to appear with your face uncovered every day. You don't. But it isn't an easy shortcut either, so let's take it step by step.

The myth of the compulsory face

There's a very common idea: to sell on social media, you have to be a "face", an influencer, someone who shows themselves completely. This idea holds some truth for certain businesses, where personality is the product. For most info products, it doesn't apply. A home organisation guide, an invoice template or a study planner are bought for what they do for the person buying them.

A face helps create connection. Connection is also built through your voice, your handwriting, the way you explain things, your consistency and the care you put into what you deliver.

Warning

Faceless doesn't mean without identity. Someone with no name, no story, no tone of voice and no particular way of seeing things doesn't build trust. You may not show your face, but you have to show that there's a real person on the other side.

The three myths that hold you back most

When I run workshops, I hear three sentences almost every time. They're worth looking at calmly.

MythWhat happens in practiceWhat to do instead
"I need to look good in photos to sell."People buy from whoever explains well, not from whoever looks good in a photo.Focus on clarity: short sentences, concrete examples, one problem solved per post.
"Nobody trusts you without a face."Trust is built through consistency, transparency and delivery.Show the process, reply to messages and do what you promised.
"I have to post every day to exist."Posting without a strategy wears you out and doesn't sell any more.Choose a rhythm you can keep up for months and stick to it.

None of these myths is about you. They describe a pattern other people have imposed on you, often without saying so.

The real advantages of faceless

I'm not selling faceless to you as the perfect solution. It has concrete advantages, which are worth knowing before you decide:

  • Privacy. You don't expose your family, your home, your workplace or your children's routine. This matters a lot if your job doesn't yet know you have a side project.
  • Simpler production. Content made with hands can be filmed in an afternoon and cut into several formats. It doesn't depend on you being in a good mood, on your hair or on studio lighting.
  • Focus on value. The attention of the viewer goes to the problem and the product, not to your appearance or to comparisons.
  • Less comparison. You don't have to compete with attractive faces or with lives that look perfect. You compete on the quality of what you deliver.

Inês is a fictional character who helps me explain this. Situations like hers are common.

Story

Illustrative case: Inês. Inês made recipe guides for friends and family. At first she posted photos of herself next to the kitchen table, and the comments were mostly about how she looked. When she started filming only her hands chopping vegetables and writing the step-by-step on screen, the questions changed. She stopped hearing "is that really you?" and started getting questions about the ingredients. The content became more useful, and attention went back to what she was teaching.

What actually sells

If you take the face out of the equation, what's left? Three things, which will come up throughout the book:

  1. The problem, properly understood. The buyer feels that someone has grasped exactly what bothers them.
  2. Proof that you can solve it. It might be the visible process, a real example of your work or a demonstration.
  3. The transformation. The person can see the path between the before and the after, without exaggerated promises.

A face is one way of showing these three things. It isn't the only one, and for many products it isn't even the most effective.

Key idea

You're not selling your face. You're selling the difference your product makes in the life of the person who buys it, and your hands are the proof that the difference is real.

You don't have to appear for people to see you. You have to show, clearly, what you do.

Maria Costa

Exercise: who is behind it?

Exercise · Who is behind the brand?
  1. Write the name you'll use for the brand. It can be your own name, a surname or a word that represents you. It doesn't have to be final.
  2. Write three words that describe the way you speak (for example: direct, calm, practical).
  3. Choose an object, a gesture or a habit that is yours and could appear in all your content (a particular mug, the way you fold paper, the green notebook).
  4. Write one sentence you would say to someone just starting out, as if you were sitting next to them at the kitchen table.

Write here:

In summary

  • A face isn't compulsory for selling info products. Clarity, consistency and delivery matter more.
  • Faceless has real advantages: privacy, simpler production and a focus on value.
  • Faceless isn't anonymity. The buyer needs to feel there's a real person behind it.
  • What sells is the problem solved, the proof of the process and the transformation of the buyer.

To do today

  1. Pick up your phone and look at the last five pieces of content you saved or watched to the end. Check which ones show hands, objects or process.
  2. Write on paper the three words you would use to describe the way you explain things.
  3. Choose a provisional name for the brand. You don't need to register it today.
  4. Prop your phone against a shelf and record twenty seconds of your hands doing a simple task. Don't publish it. You just want to see how it looks.
2

The client who comes looking for you

You don't sell to an audience. You sell to one person who, tonight, has a specific problem.

When someone starts planning a digital product, they tend to think of "women aged 25 to 40" or "entrepreneurs". These are useful categories for a presentation, but they don't help you write a sentence someone will read on their phone, on the metro. To sell, you need a real person, with a real pain and real words.

In this chapter we're going to build that person, work out what bothers them and learn to use their words, not yours.

Who the person on the other side is

Think of Sofia (illustrative example). She's thirty-two, works in an office in Lisbon, pays rent and has a schedule that starts at nine and ends when it ends. She likes cooking at the weekend, but never gets round to organising the recipes she keeps on her phone. She wants to start doing something of her own, but she's worried she won't have the time or the knack.

The detail is what matters. It isn't enough to say that Sofia "wants to earn some extra money". You need to know what she does in the evening, what tires her out, what makes her hesitate and where her free time goes. That's what lets you write something that feels as if it was written for her.

Key idea

The more concrete the person you imagine, the easier it is to write for a real person, rather than for an average that interests nobody.

Pain, desire and language

Every client has three layers you need to map:

  • The pain: what bothers them today. Tiredness, lack of time, fear of failing, the feeling of always being behind.
  • The desire: what they would like to have or feel. A project that's theirs, a lighter routine, the sense of moving forward.
  • The language: the exact words they use to talk about this. She doesn't say "I need to optimise my time". She says "I can't leave work and still do something for myself".

The third layer is the most important and the most ignored. When you write using the person's own words, they recognise themselves. When you write in jargon, they feel you're talking about something else.

PainHow the person says itDesireHow the person says it
Lack of time"I don't have the energy for this at the end of the day."Having a project of her own"I wanted to do something that was mine."
Fear of failing"What if this doesn't work and I waste my time?"Feeling she's moving forward"I wanted to see some progress, however small."
Lack of knack"I'm not good with technology."Being able to"I wanted to understand how it's done, without complications."

Where your client's language lives

Real language can't be invented. Look for it where people are already talking about the problem you solve:

  • Comments on other people's posts that cover topics similar to yours.
  • Questions people ask in groups, forums or Q&A sections.
  • Reviews of similar products, especially the critical ones. Complaints are gold dust, because they show what was missing.
  • Messages you've already received from friends and strangers about the topic.

Keep the phrases that come up most often in a list. You'll use them as titles for posts, as hooks for stories and as the basis for your DM conversations.

Warning

Don't copy other people's texts or phrases as they are. Use the pattern of the language (the type of word, the doubt, the emotion) and write your own version. Never quote someone else's comment without their permission and without anonymising it.

The empathy map

The empathy map is a sheet divided into four quadrants, which helps you put the person on paper. The quadrants are: what they think and feel, what they see, what they hear and what they say and do. At the bottom of the map you bring together the pain and the gain, that is, what they want to get rid of and what they want to achieve.

You don't need a sophisticated tool. A sheet of A4 folded in four will do. The value is in the act of writing, because it forces you to think about things you would otherwise take for granted.

Exercise · My client's empathy map
  1. Give the person a name and an age. Write one sentence about their job and their routine.
  2. Thinks and feels: what goes through her head when she wakes up? And on Sunday night?
  3. Sees: what appears in her feed? What kind of content makes her stop, and what kind makes her scroll past?
  4. Hears: what do friends, family and colleagues tell her? What advice has she received that didn't work?
  5. Says and does: what does she say out loud, in private conversations, in groups? What does she actually do when nobody is watching?
  6. Pain and gain: what's the biggest pain she wants to leave behind? What's the biggest gain she imagines?

Write here:

The offer comes from the pain, not from your taste

A very common mistake is to create a product from what we're passionate about. You love photography, so you make a "photography course". The problem is that people don't buy photography. They buy the solution to a pain.

Compare:

  • "Photography course" → a generic desire, with no urgency.
  • "Guide to ten angles for photographing food at home with your phone, without studio lights" → a specific pain, concrete language, an outcome that's easy to picture.

The second version is shorter, more honest and easier to sell, because the person recognises themselves straight away.

Warning

Don't write for everyone. Someone who tries to please everybody ends up saying nothing to anybody. A well-defined client doesn't stop others from buying, but it gives your message a recipient.

How to speak to her with your hands

This map has a practical consequence for hands-based content. If Sofia is worried she won't have the knack, show your hands doing something simple, in real time, without over-the-top cuts and with the step-by-step easy to read. If she has no time, show the process in three minutes rather than twenty. The hands don't need to talk. They need to show that the problem has a solution and that it can be done with little time.

The charts and examples you'll see throughout the book always come back to one question: who is the person, and what is pulling them away from where they are?

In summary

  • Sell to one specific person, with a specific pain and a specific desire.
  • Your client's words are worth more than yours. Collect them where they already exist.
  • The empathy map makes you think about what the person sees, hears, says and does.
  • An offer is born from a specific pain, not from your personal taste.

To do today

  1. Write the name, age and job of the person you want to help. One sentence is enough.
  2. Fill in the six lines of the empathy map, on paper or in a note on your phone.
  3. Open a group or forum where your topic is discussed and copy three real questions into your list of phrases.
  4. Today, send a message to a trusted person who isn't family and ask: "What's the thing that costs you most about this topic?" Listen to the answer without correcting it.
3

A brand without a face

A brand without a face needs a face made of habits: the colour, the lettering, the voice and the gesture that repeat.

When no face appears, identity starts living somewhere else. It moves into the background colour, the font of the headline, the way you write a "thank you" and the object that always sits on the same table. If none of this is defined, every post seems to come from a different person, and anyone following you feels lost.

This chapter is about making that identity exist on purpose. You don't need an expensive designer or an agency. You need simple decisions, made once, and the discipline to keep repeating them.

What faceless identity is

Identity is, at heart, whatever repeats. In a faceless brand it usually rests on four pillars:

  1. Colour palette, the set of colours you always use.
  2. Typography, the typefaces you choose for headlines and body text.
  3. Voice, the way you speak, your vocabulary and your tone.
  4. Visual signature, the recurring elements that identify you: the hands, the objects, the camera angle and the style of text on screen.

None of these pillars is a work of art. They are choices made for consistency.

Palette

Choose three colours: one for the background, one for the highlight and one neutral for secondary text. Before you decide, check that the text reads well against the background, especially on a phone in the sun.

An illustrative example: a cream background, dark brown text and a moss green for buttons and call-to-action arrows. These three colours feel calm and work well with photos of hands and natural materials. You don't need to copy this example. Choose what fits the way you are.

Warning

Don't choose colours just because they're trendy this month. A palette that changes from week to week is one nobody recognises. Change it only when you have a clear reason and the decision is written down.

Typography

Use two fonts at most: one for headlines, with more personality, and another for body text, cleaner and easier to read. There are good free options. What matters is size: on a phone screen, small text is tiring and people leave.

A practical rule: if you have to bring the screen closer to read it, make the letters bigger. If the text fills more than half the screen in a short video, cut words.

Voice

Voice is the hardest part to define and the one that carries the most weight for trust. Choose three adjectives and, for each one, write an example sentence and a sentence you would never say.

AdjectiveI would sayI would not say
Direct"This guide answers the overtime question in three steps.""Maybe this guide could, in some way, help."
Calm"No rush. One step at a time.""Buy now or you'll lose everything!"
Practical"Here's the template. Copy it and adapt it.""Imagine every possibility in the universe."

Also pay attention to the words you use to greet, thank and say goodbye. These little phrases repeat a lot, and they say more about you than a logo does.

Key idea

Voice isn't what you say in a single post. It's what people hear from you after ten posts in a row.

Visual signature: the hands

In a faceless brand, the hands are your signature. But hands only work as a signature when they appear repeatedly. Choose:

  • The table. Always the same one, or the same work surface. It can be a wooden tabletop or a smooth tablecloth.
  • The light. Always the same source, ideally natural light from a window early in the morning or late in the afternoon.
  • The recurring object. A particular pen, a notebook, a mug. It's the element people start to recognise.
  • The point of view. Film from the angle of your eyes when you're working. Viewers feel they're sitting beside you.
  • The on-screen text. Always the same typeface, the same position and the same size for key phrases.

This list might seem excessive, but it isn't. When someone sees three seconds of hands on a green notebook and knows it's your brand, the identity is already working.

Exercise: my signature

Exercise · My visual signature
  1. Choose three colours. Write the name of each one and, if you know it, the hex code.
  2. Choose two fonts: one for headlines and one for body text. Check that they are free or that you already have a licence to use them.
  3. Write three adjectives for your voice. Beside each one, write a sentence you would say and a sentence you wouldn't.
  4. Choose an object, a gesture and a surface that will appear in all your content.
  5. Take a test photo of your hands in that setting, using the light you have at home, and save it as a reference.

Write here:

In summary

  • A brand without a face lives on repetition: colour, lettering, voice and visual signature.
  • Choose three colours and two fonts at most, and check they read well on a phone.
  • Voice is defined with adjectives, examples and clear limits.
  • Hands only work as a signature when they always appear in the same setting.

To do today

  1. Open your notes app and write down the three colours you'll use, with the code if you know it. If you don't, choose by eye and save them.
  2. Pick a headline font from a free typography site and check that it reads well on a phone.
  3. Take a photo of your hands on the table you have, in today's light, and save it in the "Brand" folder.
  4. Write three adjectives for your voice, and beside each one a sentence you would say.
4

Your first digital product

You don't need the perfect product. You need the first one that someone wants enough to write to you about.

There's a classic trap for beginners: spending months planning a huge course, with ten modules, bonuses, videos with good lighting and a flawless sales page, and never launching anything. When it finally launches, they don't know whether anyone needs it, because they never asked.

Your first digital product is there to teach you. It should be small, clear and made with care, but it doesn't have to be complete. In this chapter you'll see the most common types of product, how to validate them before you build them, and how to think about a ladder of value that gives you room to grow.

What a digital product is

A digital product is content you deliver without stock, without shipping and without packaging. It can be a file to download, access to a private area, a set of videos or a template the person uses on their computer. You sell it once, or by subscription, and it can be delivered automatically.

That nature is a huge advantage: the cost of delivering one more copy is almost zero. But it also has a downside. Because there's nothing physical, all the value has to sit in how clearly you describe what you're offering.

The most common types

The table below compares the most used formats. The timings are only rough orders of magnitude, because they depend heavily on your availability and how complex the topic is.

TypeWhat it is forRough time to createExample
E-bookGoing deeper into a topic with text and imagesA few weeksBalcony vegetable garden guide for beginners
TemplateSaving time with a ready-to-use modelA few daysContent planning template for the month
Pocket guide or checklistSolving one specific stepA few hoursChecklist for posting a story without mistakes
PlannerOrganising a routineA few daysWeekly planner for shift workers
Mini-courseTeaching a process in stagesA few weeksFour short lessons on making simple invoices

No format is better in the abstract. The best one is the format that solves your person's problem, within the time you have to build it.

Validate before you build

Validating means confirming that someone wants something before you spend weeks making it. There are simple ways to do this:

  1. Ask ten people. Don't ask "do you think you would buy it?", because everyone says yes. Ask: "When did you last try to sort this out? What did you do?"
  2. Create a waiting list. A simple page or a form where people leave their email to say they want to hear when it's ready. If nobody signs up, you've learnt something.
  3. Sell the small version first. If you already have a part ready, offer it at a low price with clear delivery. If you have nothing yet, be open about the delivery timeline.
Warning

If you charge for something that doesn't exist yet, say clearly what will be delivered, when and how. Never take payment for a product you don't have and can't deliver. This is a matter of honesty and, in many cases, of consumer protection.

Warning

Don't build a ten-module course before you know whether anyone wants the first one. Almost always, the first product should be half of what you'd planned.

I'm not asking you for a perfect product. I'm asking for one that someone uses and that tells you what's missing.

Maria Costa

The ladder of value

A ladder of value is the sequence of products and touchpoints that takes someone from first contact to the most complete product. You don't have to build it all at once. But having the ladder drawn helps you see where your first product fits.

The rungs usually look like this:

  • The free lead magnet. A short guide or checklist that answers one small question. It lets the person try your way of teaching.
  • The entry product. A template or guide at a low price that solves one specific problem.
  • The core product. A mini-course or a more in-depth e-book, for people who want to go further.
  • The follow-up. A community, a mentoring programme or meetups, for people who want support.

A free lead magnet isn't a gift with no purpose. It collects the email of whoever asks for it, with consent, and gives you the chance to explain the next step.

How to choose the first one

To choose your first product, answer four questions honestly:

QuestionIf the answer is no
Do I know this well enough to teach it?Study more or pick another topic.
Are there people looking for this solution?Validate with questions before you go ahead.
Can I deliver in about thirty days?Narrow the scope until you can.
Does it fit into my week without burning me out?Simplify the format.
Story

Illustrative case: Rui. Rui is a fictional character. He spent two months planning a complete photography course. When he asked a few people what was holding them back, he heard something different: they wanted to photograph the products in their online shops with their phones and didn't know where to start. Rui wrote a twelve-page guide on exactly that. It wasn't the course he'd imagined, but it was the first product people asked him for back, with questions and doubts. That's how he worked out what to build next.

Exercise: choose your first product

Exercise · My first product
  1. Write three product ideas. For each one, note the format (e-book, template, guide, planner or mini-course).
  2. For each idea, write the specific problem it solves, in one sentence, using the words of the person who has it.
  3. Run the validation: write the questions you'll ask ten people and note the date you'll ask them.
  4. Pick one of the ideas using the four questions in the table. The one with the most yeses is your front-runner.
  5. Sketch your ladder of value in three rungs: free lead magnet, entry product and core product.

Write here:

In summary

  • Your first product should be small, clear and validated. It doesn't need to be complete.
  • The most common formats are the e-book, the template, the pocket guide, the planner and the mini-course.
  • Validate with open questions, a waiting list or a small version.
  • The ladder of value shows you where your first product fits in the person's path.
  • I'm not promising the first product will bring in money by the end of the month. Results depend on each person's effort.

To do today

  1. Write three product ideas in your phone's notes, each with the problem it solves in one sentence.
  2. Send the questions from the validation card to three people today, by message. You don't need ten to start.
  3. Create a free form with name, email and one sentence saying what you're preparing. Include a consent line so you can get in touch.
  4. Draw the three rungs of the ladder on a sheet of paper: free lead magnet, entry product and core product. It doesn't need to look pretty.
5

Content with AI

AI writes drafts. The person who decides what's true, and what sounds like you, is you.

Some people think AI will do everything on its own and that all you need is to press a button. Others are scared of any new tool and refuse to try it. Both positions are not much use to anyone who wants to sell without showing up.

In this chapter I'll show you a sensible way to use AI for content: as an assistant, with a clear workflow and human review at every step. AI helps you think faster. It doesn't think for you.

AI as an assistant, not an author

The golden rule is simple: AI isn't the author. It's an assistant that gives you options, organises ideas and speeds up repetitive tasks. The authorship, the experience and the responsibility for what you publish are yours.

In practice, this means that:

  • You never publish a generated text without reading it, correcting it and adding something of your own.
  • You always check the facts, dates, numbers and names the tool gives you.
  • You don't use AI to create client testimonials, screenshots of results or quotes from real people.
  • When AI suggests something that sounds like a promise, you rewrite the sentence into something true and measured.
Warning

Never publish testimonials, results or numbers that AI has made up. If it didn't happen, it doesn't exist. It's the quickest way to lose the trust of the people who follow you, and it can cause legal problems, especially in advertising and commercial practices.

The four-step workflow

Content almost always goes through four stages: idea, script, design and publishing. At each one, AI can help, but the final decision is yours.

1. Idea. Gather twenty real questions your clients have asked. Ask AI to group them by theme and suggest different angles for each group. You choose three.

2. Script. Ask for a simple structure: hook, problem, step, close. Then write the text yourself, in your own words. If AI gives you a good sentence, rewrite it the way you would say it.

3. Design. Use AI to generate visual variations based on your palette and your typography. She Is Studio is the AI design studio from She Is Faceless Academy: it helps you create visual pieces that line up with your identity, trying out and comparing options. Always choose the one that feels most like you.

4. Publishing. Schedule it, read the final version out loud and confirm the time. This stage is human from start to finish.

A prompt that works

A good prompt gives context, sets the tone and asks for a specific format. This template is an example. Adapt it to your own situation:

`` Act as a copywriter for a faceless brand, writing in British English. Tone: direct, calm, practical. Address the reader as "you". No income promises. Audience: [describe the person in two sentences]. Real doubt they have: [paste the exact sentence you heard]. Ask for: three hooks of up to ten words, and a 60-second script with on-screen text, in five short blocks. ``

In the prompt, you don't ask for results, you don't ask for numbers and you don't ask for urgency. If you do, the tool makes them up, and you spend your time cleaning up.

Review before you publish

Before you press the button, go through this table. It takes two minutes and avoids most mistakes.

StepReview question
FactsHas every number, date and name been confirmed?
ToneDoes it sound like me, or like a machine imitating me?
IdentityAre the colour, lettering and visual signature right?
PromisesIs there any sentence that promises money, results or false urgency?
PeopleHas anyone recognisable appeared without permission?
LegalIs there a disclaimer where the topic requires one?
Key idea

AI shortens the route to the draft. Review is what turns the draft into something you can sign your name to.

Exercise: test the workflow

Exercise · One piece of content, start to finish
  1. Choose a real doubt you've heard from someone.
  2. Use the prompt above (or your own) and ask for three hooks.
  3. Choose the hook that sounds most like you and write the 60-second script in your own words, without copying the AI.
  4. Compare your script with the AI draft. Underline the sentences that are yours and cross out the generic ones.
  5. Review it with the table above. Mark the points where you had to correct something.

Write here:

In summary

  • AI is an assistant. The authorship and the responsibility are yours.
  • The workflow has four stages: idea, script, design and publishing.
  • A good prompt gives context, tone and format, and doesn't ask for results or numbers.
  • Never publish testimonials, numbers or results that AI has made up.

To do today

  1. Write in your phone a real doubt you've heard from someone, word for word.
  2. Ask AI for three hooks using the prompt in this chapter, changing only the audience and the doubt.
  3. Choose one hook and rewrite it in your own words, by hand, in your notebook.
  4. Read the text out loud before you schedule it, and confirm the facts with a source you can show.
6

Formats that sell without a face

The hand enters the screen, and the person decides in three seconds whether to stay or scroll past.

Think of Inês, 29, who makes paper planners at home in a small flat in Setúbal. On her first attempt she filmed herself facing the camera, explaining the product, with her phone propped on a tin of beans. Hardly anyone stopped. The following week she filmed only her hands folding a page and writing the date at the top, without saying a word. That video started more conversations than the first one. The product was the same. The format changed.

When someone asks me "what kind of video should I make?", the honest answer is that it depends on what you want the person to do next. Watch to the end, save, understand, click or write to you. Each of these actions calls for a different format.

Six formats for hands

1. Hand B-roll. Close-up shots: hands writing in a notebook, folding paper, assembling a box. It's supporting material that shows the process without needing any speech.

2. Voiceover. Your narration over footage of hands. It's useful for teaching and for explaining the reasoning behind a gesture. Record somewhere without echo, with the phone about twenty centimetres from your mouth.

3. On-screen text. Big phrases, little text per screen, which can be read without sound. Use it for the hook and for the call to action. Plenty of people watch videos with the sound off, so the text has to work on its own.

4. Carousels. A sequence of images, with one step per slide. Good for saving and sharing. A well-made carousel is a small lesson the person keeps for later.

5. POV. The camera in the position of your eyes. The viewer feels they're doing it with you. Good for short tutorials and for showing the order of a gesture.

6. Process ASMR. Natural sounds from the work: pencil scratching, paper turning, water running. It creates atmosphere and focus. Overdoing it sounds like an advert, so use it sparingly.

Format and goal matrix

Read the matrix across and choose the format that fits the intention of the day.

In pocket version:

GoalFormatWhy
Reach new peopleReel with on-screen textThe hook holds attention without sound.
Show the processB-roll with voiceoverThe person sees how the product comes to life.
Teach a step-by-stepCarouselIt gets saved and is easy to revisit.
Build closenessBehind-the-scenes POVThe person feels they're with you.
Lead to actionSequence of storiesIt lets people reply and ask for help (chapter 07).

Film once, publish in several formats

A one-hour session in which you put a product together with your hands can give you a short Reel, a six-step carousel and five stories with different details. That's seven pieces from a single moment of work. The numbers are an illustrative example, but the reasoning is real: the filming session is the expensive resource, and everything else is reuse.

Key idea

Film once and publish in several formats. The same product appears from different angles without you having to start from scratch every week.

Filming with a phone

You don't need expensive kit. You need light, a plain background and steadiness. A window with natural light will do, as long as the sun isn't hitting your hands directly. Always use the same surface, because it's going to be your visual signature. Film landscape for presentations and portrait for Reels and stories.

Sound is what people notice most. In a room with echo, a cloth or a cushion nearby helps a lot.

Warning

Don't use copyrighted music outside the libraries the platform provides for commercial use. If anyone appears in the shot, even just a familiar hand or a distinctive bracelet, ask for permission before you publish. A person's image belongs to them, and the GDPR (the EU data protection law) protects the data that makes them identifiable.

Script for a hands Reel (illustrative example)

This script is for a video of about thirty seconds on organising a to-do list.

SecondsShotOn-screen textVoiceover
0 to 3Hands opening a notebook"Too many tasks in your head?""When the list only exists in your head, it wears you out."
3 to 10B-roll: hands writing three tasks"Step 1: write everything down""Write it all down, without filtering."
10 to 20POV: hands crossing out what isn't urgent"Step 2: separate the urgent""Does this really have to be done today?"
20 to 27Hands marking three priorities"Step 3: pick three""Three, and no more. That way they fit into the day."
27 to 30Fixed shot of the notebook with the final list"I've saved this for tomorrow""If you want the template, tell me in the comments."

The last shot invites conversation without pushing. It's the kind of ending that makes people reply.

In summary

Each format serves a different goal: reach, process, teaching, closeness or action. Hands work well when the setting and the light repeat. Film once and reuse the session. And always ask for permission before anyone recognisable appears.

To do today

  1. Pick up your notebook or a sheet of paper and write, in one sentence, the goal of your next piece of content.
  2. Choose a format from the matrix that serves that goal.
  3. Film three shots of hands, with your phone propped against a box or a book, each lasting five seconds.
  4. Write the text for each shot, with no more than seven words per line.
  5. Watch the three shots without sound. If you can't tell what's happening, reshoot before you publish.
7

Stories that sell

A story doesn't sell on its own. It sells once the person already feels at home with you.

Think of Duarte, 34, who sells hand-made recipe notebooks in Braga. He was posting beautiful stories, with photos of the pages and the right music, and nobody replied. One afternoon he noticed that the stories with the most replies were the ones that ended with a simple question. He changed only the ending of each sequence, and conversations started to appear on their own. It wasn't a technical trick. It was putting the question in the right place.

Stories disappear after a few hours, so people look at them with a different kind of attention. It's a more intimate space than the feed. Anyone watching a story is looking into your day, your table and your hands in a real moment. That's an opportunity, and also a responsibility.

Why the sequence matters

A post reaches a lot of people at once and then sinks among the others. A story reaches people who already follow you, usually appears at the top of the list and allows a direct reply. But a single story can be lovely and say nothing. Five stories with a clear logic build a small path, from interest to action.

The five-story sequence

The sequence has five steps: hook, problem, proof, offer and action. These are Duarte's examples. Adapt them to your product, your number of pages and the way you deliver.

Story 1, the hook. Hands placing a pen on the table. It's there to catch the people who already follow you.

Story 2, the problem. Hands flicking through a notebook full of lists. It shows that you understand what the person is feeling. If you want to add a voiceover, something like "when we try to do everything at once, tiredness arrives fast."

Story 3, the proof. Hands putting together the first version of the guide. It shows process, never results you can't show.

Story 4, the offer. Hands showing the guide open on the screen. It presents the product clearly.

Story 5, the action. Hands typing a message on the phone. It asks for one specific reply, and only one.

Story 3 doesn't say "I sold so much" or "I earned so much". It shows a real process. If you don't yet have a process to show, show the path you're on, without making anything up.

Warning

Never use fake countdowns, or "last spots" when it isn't true. Invented urgency wears out the people following you and can count as an unfair commercial practice.

Question and poll stickers

A question sticker asks the person to write their biggest doubt about the topic. A two-option poll tells you, in seconds, which pain is most common. Use these answers as raw material. They are the real language I talked about in chapter 02, and they form the basis for your next post or your next product.

Key idea

Stickers are the simplest way to hear your client. Every reply is a clue for your next piece of content.

When someone replies

When someone replies to a story, the conversation starts. The rule is simple: thank them, ask a question and only then talk about the product. That's how Duarte built the habit, and the conversation below shows the same movement.

Chapter 08 goes deeper into these conversations and shows how to move forward without sounding like a sales pitch.

A story isn't an advert. It's a conversation that starts with someone looking at you.

Maria Costa
Story

Illustrative case: Teresa. Teresa, a fictional person, created meal-planning templates. At first she posted beautiful stories, but with no question at the end, and almost nobody replied. She changed two things: she started using a question sticker in each sequence and writing a specific invitation in the last story. Replies became more frequent and more useful, and, in people's own words, she could see which topics should come first in her next template.

In summary

A story works like a conversation, and the five-step sequence takes the person from interest to action. Show real process in the proof and never invent results or urgency. Stickers are the best way to hear from the people following you. And the first reply should be a question.

To do today

  1. Choose a topic you've already worked on in the earlier chapters and write it in one sentence on your phone.
  2. Write the five lines of the sequence: hook, problem, proof, offer and action.
  3. Film the five stories with your phone propped against a box or a book, each with five or six seconds of hands.
  4. Add a question sticker to the second story and a poll sticker to the last one.
  5. Publish all five on the same day and reply to every response within the next two hours.
8

The DM that doesn't feel like a sales pitch

A private message is a door. Knock, and wait to be invited in.

Think of Marta, 38, who sells a mini sewing course for beginners. One day she received a message from a stranger with a link, three exclamation marks and the word "TODAY" in capitals. She deleted it without reading to the end. The offer might well have been good. It was the form that put her off.

The direct message is where a sale looks most like a conversation, and where most people get it wrong. Either they write coldly, with a copy-and-paste message everyone recognises, or they're so afraid of bothering anyone that they never say what they're offering. Both drive away people who could have been clients.

This chapter teaches you to sell by DM in an ethical way: no spam, no pressure, and respect for each person's decision.

Ask before you send

The conversation starts with permission. There are two ways this can happen. The person has interacted with you first, with a comment, a reply to a story or a request for information. Or you asked permission before sending the offer: "Can I send you the guide by message?"

If neither of these situations exists, don't send anything. You can post, reply to public comments, or create a way for people to come to you. The cold, mass DM is the shortest route to being blocked and to a bad reputation.

Warning

Sending the same message to two hundred people with no connection is spam. It can lead to reports, account restrictions and a loss of trust from the people following you. It can also breach data protection rules.

The DM funnel

A sales conversation has stages, and rushing usually costs you. Each stage has its own timing.

The five stages are: interaction, permission, conversation, offer and decision. The person buys, thinks it over or says no, and any of these answers is valid.

Conversations that feel like conversations

These conversations are illustrative examples. Read them out loud before you use them, and swap the words for your own.

The first one starts with a comment on a video. Marta asks permission before sending the guide.

The second shows a price objection. The reply doesn't argue about money. It offers a smaller first step.

The third is a follow-up three days later, followed by a graceful exit. The person didn't reply, and the final message closes the door politely.

And now what not to do. This is an example of a cold message, sent to someone who has never spoken to you.

The message has no question, no context and no way out. The person receiving it feels they were picked from a list. So don't copy this model, not even to "test" it.

Follow-up without being annoying

Follow-up is the part most people are afraid to do, and the part most people do badly. Simple rules: no more than two follow-ups per person, spaced a few days apart. Each one brings something new, such as a detail, an answer to a doubt or a different example. And if the person says no, you thank them and finish.

MomentMessageGoal
Day 0Gentle offerOpen the conversation about the offer
Day 3Follow-up with a questionRemind them without pressure
Day 7Gentle exitClose with respect
Story

Illustrative case: Afonso. Afonso, a fictional person, used to send long messages full of explanations to anyone who asked him for the guide. The conversations were good, but hardly anyone moved forward. When he started asking just one discovery question before talking about the product, he realised people had doubts very different from the ones he'd imagined. He adjusted the offer to those doubts, and the conversations became shorter, clearer and more honest.

Consent and GDPR in a few lines

If you collect emails or contacts, you have to be transparent about what you'll do with them. Say who you are, why you want the contact and how often you'll write. Ask for clear agreement, for example with a tick box that isn't pre-ticked. Always offer an easy way out, and don't keep more data than you need.

For an assessment of your specific case, speak to a lawyer. Here you'll only find the general logic.

To do today

  1. Open your recent interactions (comments and replies to stories) and write a list of the people who have already spoken to you.
  2. Reply to each one with a question, without mentioning the product yet.
  3. Write a reply script for people who commented, in your own words, and save it in your phone's notes.
  4. Write your exit message. If you can write it calmly, your DM rule is ready.
  5. Don't send anything to someone who hasn't spoken to you. If you're unsure, ask first whether they'd like to receive it.
9

More sources of income

More channels mean more paths, and also more things to look after. Choose one at a time.

Think of Henrique, 36, who has had a digital product running for two months. One week he decided to open a shop on a marketplace, start a book, take on content work for brands and offer design services. At the end of a month he hadn't done any of them properly. He was tired, with four tabs open and none of them moving forward.

The temptation is strong. It seems sensible to spread the risk. In practice, spreading your attention across many channels tends to divide your time without multiplying it. In this chapter you'll see four options, the pros and cons of each, and a way to decide where to start. There are no promises here, only honest questions.

Before you diversify

Diversifying makes sense once you have a foundation. That foundation can be a product validated by real people (chapter 04), a content routine you've kept up for a few weeks (chapter 06), or a way of talking to the people following you without feeling overwhelmed (chapter 08). If you don't have any of these yet, a new channel will take away the time you need to consolidate what you already have.

The four options

Marketplaces for digital products and crafts. Platforms where people look for ready-made products, such as templates, prints or kits. They usually charge fees per listing and per sale, which change over time. Always check the terms on the official page before you decide.

E-books and print on demand. You publish a book with no stock, because printing happens as orders come in. Royalties depend on the price, the format and the market, and a title's success depends heavily on the niche, the title and the cover.

UGC (content created for brands). Making videos and photos that brands use on their own channels. It's paid per project and requires a portfolio, meeting deadlines and good communication. It isn't passive income. It's creative work on commission.

Digital services. Offering work such as social media management, design, copywriting or document organisation to individuals or businesses. It's the option that looks most like traditional service provision, with contracts, invoicing and a direct relationship with the client.

Side-by-side comparison

OptionStrengthsWatch out forBest suited to
MarketplacePeople already searching for that type of productFees, competition and little contact with buyersAnyone with simple, repeatable products
E-book or print on demandA product that stays available for a long timeA lot of writing and cover work before the first saleAnyone with a niche topic who enjoys writing
UGCHands-on experience with brands and professional contentDepends on orders and a portfolioAnyone already comfortable filming and editing
Digital servicesDirect income and a close relationship with the clientWorking time is directly tied to incomeAnyone with a well-established skill

This is how to read the table without fooling yourself. The strengths are real, but none of them takes the work off your plate.

Warning

There's no such thing as a passive channel. All of them demand creation time, attention to the page, replies to clients and reviewing rules that change. Be wary of anyone who sells you a channel as if it weren't work.

Tax and legal framework

Selling products or providing services, even online, usually brings tax and invoicing obligations in Portugal. This includes setting up your activity, issuing invoices and declaring your income on the IRS (Portugal's annual income tax return). The rules change, and the right setup depends on your specific situation. Don't make these decisions off the top of your head.

Speak to a certified accountant (contabilista certificado) before you start invoicing. An initial consultation is a small investment compared with the cost of sorting out a badly handled situation.

If the answer to the first question is no, the new channel won't solve the problem. It will only split your time further.

How to decide

Answer these questions honestly, one option at a time:

  1. Do I already have skills someone pays for, without having to learn them from scratch?
  2. How many hours a week can I give this channel without taking time from the routine I already have?
  3. Can I keep going for at least three months before I know whether it makes sense?
  4. Does this channel depend entirely on me, or does it depend on third parties, such as platforms or brands?
  5. Do I know where this channel's tax obligations sit, and who can help me organise them?

Results depend on each person's effort. No channel guarantees any amount, and the table is there to help you think, not to make promises.

In summary

Diversify when you already have a validated base, not to escape a problem you haven't solved yet. Each channel needs time for creation, maintenance and attention. Tax and invoicing are part of the business. And choose one channel at a time, with your criteria defined before you start.

To do today

  1. Write the four options on a sheet of paper, one per line.
  2. Answer the five questions in the "How to decide" section for each option, with a yes or a no.
  3. Estimate how many hours a week you'd need to give each one over the first three months, without taking time from what you already have.
  4. Choose a single option to test over the next ninety days.
  5. Write in your phone, with the date, what has to happen for you to decide whether to carry on or stop.
10

The business that fits into your life

Head, body and heart. A business that doesn't fit into your life ends up eating it.

There's a version of online entrepreneurship that sells the idea that you can always be working, sleep very little and call it passion. That isn't what I'm proposing. I want to talk to you about a business that fits into your life: one that respects your time, your health and the things that give you meaning.

It's often called a lifestyle business. It's a business designed around the pace of life you want to have, not one that grows at any cost. Be honest with yourself: it isn't a business without work. It's work with limits.

What a lifestyle business is

A lifestyle business has three characteristics. It grows at a pace the person can sustain. It puts sustainability ahead of speed. And it has clear limits, set before the pressure arrives.

These limits might look like a way of holding back growth. In practice, they stop the business from becoming a second load you never switch off from. Someone who doesn't define the end of the day ends up working every hour there is.

Head, body and heart

I think of a sustainable business as a balance between three dimensions. If one of them dominates the others, the rest start to give way.

DimensionWhat it asks forQuestions to ask yourself
HeadPlanning, strategy and learningWhat am I learning this week? What have I decided with clarity?
BodySleep, breaks, movement and a calm spaceAm I sleeping enough? Do I have a place where I work and where I stop working?
HeartMeaning, enjoyment and saying no to what drains youWhat gives me energy in this work? What am I starting to hate?
Key idea

A healthy business isn't the one that grows fastest. It's the one you can keep going for years without losing your health or your desire to do it.

I'm not asking you to work more. I'm asking you to work within the time you've chosen.

Maria Costa

A typical week

A simple way to make sure the business fits into your life is to sketch out a typical week. It isn't a rigid timetable. It's a way of seeing where the work blocks sit and where the breaks are.

This is an illustrative example for someone who works a full-time job and gives the project about seven hours a week (the table adds up to 6h 45min, rounded):

DayBlockTime (example)
MondayPlan the week's content1 hour
TuesdayFilm hands, one session for several formats1 hour 30min
WednesdayWrite scripts and stories1 hour
ThursdayWork on the product2 hours
FridayReply to messages and DM conversations45 minutes
SaturdayShort review and scheduled publishing30 minutes
SundayNo work0

Sunday is left blank on purpose. If the business needs Sunday to function, then the business is designing your life, and that's a signal to adjust what you do.

There's no income promise in this chapter. Results depend on each person's effort, their time and the way they organise their week.

Tools to see what you actually did

Good planning only helps if you can later see what really happened. She Is Daily is the planning app from my brand, and it's built for exactly that: you put the blocks of your week in the right place and, at the end, see how long each thing took and what was left undone.

You don't need a specific tool for this review. A notebook with three columns (what I planned, what I did, what I learnt) will do. What matters is the habit of reviewing.

Limits that protect the business

Limits are the most practical part of this chapter. Define them in writing and communicate them to your buyers when it's relevant.

Warning

If you're always available, the client learns to expect that you are. Limits aren't a punishment for the buyer. They're an honest way of keeping up the quality of what you deliver.

Story

Illustrative case: Tiago. Tiago, a fictional person, worked as an employee and had about an hour and a half a night for his project. At first he replied to every message straight away, even at night, and within a few weeks he felt exhausted. When he set a reply window and a day without work, the project slowed down but gained in quality. The problem wasn't the time. It was the lack of boundaries.

In summary

A lifestyle business grows at a pace you can sustain, and it has both work and limits. Balance head, body and heart, because when one dimension dominates, the others give way. Sketch out a typical week and set aside one day without work, even if it seems impossible.

To do today

  1. Open the calendar on your phone and write down the hours you actually have each week for the project, after your job, your home and your rest.
  2. Sketch your typical week in a phone note, with one block per task and one empty day.
  3. Choose the time you close off work each day and create an alarm with that name.
  4. Write your reply hours in one line and paste it into your profile description.
  5. Choose your day without work and, on that day, don't open your phone for the project.
11

The 30-day plan

Thirty days won't cover everything. They're enough to start well and to see the path ahead of you.

We've reached the end of the book. If you've read each chapter with your notebook open, you already have plenty to work with: a specific person in mind, a brand with colour, lettering and voice, a first product you've validated, a sequence of stories, DM scripts and a week that fits into your life.

This last chapter brings it all together into a thirty-day plan, with a launch checklist and a glossary so you don't get lost in the words of digital marketing. It isn't a plan to follow to the letter. It's a map. If one day doesn't work out, adjust and carry on.

How to use this plan

The plan is split into four parts, each with its own focus. Each day has one main task, which should fit into thirty to sixty minutes. If you have a day with less time, do the minimum version and log it in your notebook. A small day done is worth more than a big day that never happened.

Within each part the order isn't a big deal, but the order between parts matters. Don't jump to the next part before you've finished the previous one.

Part 1 · Client and rest (days 1 to 7)

  • Day 1: write your starting point on one page, without editing it.
  • Day 2: choose the provisional name and the three words for your voice.
  • Day 3: fill in the empathy map for one specific person.
  • Day 4: collect ten real phrases about the pain (comments, questions, messages).
  • Day 5: describe the offer in terms of that pain, in one sentence.
  • Day 6: review what you've learnt and write down two product hypotheses.
  • Day 7: rest. Read through your notes and don't work on the project.

Part 2 · Brand and first product (days 8 to 18)

  • Day 8: choose your three colours and two fonts.
  • Day 9: define the table, the light and the object of your signature.
  • Day 10: take the test photo of your hands and review it.
  • Day 11: write the three adjectives for your voice, with examples.
  • Day 12: complete the brand checklist.
  • Day 13: ask ten people the validation questions.
  • Day 14: analyse the answers and choose a format.
  • Day 15: write the product outline in five points.
  • Day 16: write the first part of the product.
  • Day 17: sketch the ladder of value in three rungs.
  • Day 18: prepare the free lead magnet, short and useful.

Part 3 · Content, stories and DMs (days 19 to 27)

  • Day 19: gather twenty real doubts and group them by theme.
  • Day 20: write three hooks and rewrite them in your own style.
  • Day 21: film a session of hands for several formats.
  • Day 22: publish a thirty-second Reel with on-screen text.
  • Day 23: publish a six-step carousel.
  • Day 24: write the five-story sequence.
  • Day 25: publish the sequence, with a question sticker.
  • Day 26: write your three scripts (reply, discovery and exit).
  • Day 27: reply to all the interactions from the last few days.

Part 4 · System and review (days 28 to 30)

  • Day 28: sketch your typical week and set the day without work.
  • Day 29: write your three limits down and communicate the relevant ones.
  • Day 30: review the thirty days and choose the next step.
Warning

Don't change product, colour and channel every day. Thirty days without changing direction are worth more than thirty days starting new things.

Launch checklist

Before you announce the product, confirm each point. If one isn't done, it's not a failure. It's a sign to put the launch back by a week.

  • The product is finished and reviewed by someone you trust.
  • The price is set and written clearly, with no small print.
  • You know how the person receives the product (file, link, access) and you've tested that route.
  • The description says who the product is for, what it is and what it isn't.
  • There's a clear sentence saying that results depend on each person's effort.
  • If you've collected contacts, consent is recorded and there's a way to leave the list.
  • You have template replies for the most common questions.
  • You have a set day and time to launch, and a reply window.
  • You know what you'll do if the launch goes worse than you hoped.

My 30-day review

Reread your notebook from day 1. Write down three things you did that you're going to keep. Write down three things that didn't go as you expected, and why, honestly. Write down what you've learnt about your client, in the words you heard. Finally, choose one single next step for the next thirty days.

Glossary

The terms below appear throughout the book. If any of them seems unfamiliar, come back here.

  • Visual signature. The set of recurring elements (table, light, object, angle) that identify the brand.
  • B-roll. Supporting shots, usually close-ups, that illustrate a process without dialogue.
  • Call to action (CTA). The specific request you make at the end of a piece of content.
  • Consent. A person's clear and voluntary agreement to receive messages or to have their data kept.
  • DM. A direct, private message between two people on a social network.
  • Ladder of value. The sequence of products and touchpoints, from the free one to the most complete.
  • Faceless. Literally "without a face". A brand where the content shows hands, process and product, not the face of the person making it.
  • Follow-up. A message sent after a conversation, to resume contact respectfully.
  • Hook. The first line or first shot of a piece of content, which has to hold attention in a few seconds.
  • Lead magnet. Free content, such as a guide or a checklist, that lets the person try your way of teaching.
  • Lifestyle business. A business designed around the pace of life the person wants to have, with defined limits.
  • POV. Point of view: footage shot from the angle of the eyes of the person doing the action.
  • GDPR. The General Data Protection Regulation, which governs the collection and use of personal data in the European Union.
  • UGC. Content created by creators for brands, which the brands use on their own channels.
  • Validation. Confirming, before you build, that there is real demand for what you plan to offer.
  • Voiceover. Recorded narration that accompanies images, without the person appearing on screen.

A final word

I wrote this book for anyone who wants to sell without showing up, but above all for anyone who wants to start with their hands. My hands appear in a lot of my content, and yours will appear in yours. I ask you to begin with something small, to do it with care and to show it honestly.

Learn the strategy. Build the asset. Create income.

Maria Costa
